speechtext:
My hon. friend gave me
notice of his intention to ask this question, and I sent immediately for the communications to which it was supposed to have reference. His question asks to have made public the reply to a telegram of June 3. I have no telegram of June 3, from Hon. Mr. Aberhart, but I believe the telegram to which my hon. friend refers is one of June 4. My reply is dated June 6. The telegram of June 4 is as follows:
Calgary, Alberta,
June 4, 1938.
The Right Hon. Lyon Mackenzie King,
Ottawa, Ont.
This government has been advised of several instances in which local managers of banks have informed residents that unless the existing laws in regard to certain taxation are disallowed or withdrawn branch banks throughout the province will be closed. The matter is being investigated at this end but as your government claims complete jurisdiction over banks and banking I must point out that this action of the banks has serious implications. Firstly it could be interpreted as a coercive threat to the people of Alberta and directed against his majesty's government in this province. Secondly the withdrawal of an essential service will place this government in a position of being forced to take such action as may be necessary to safeguard the welfare of our people. The banks are under definite obligation to serve the people and it is the duty of your government to see that such obligation is adequately discharged or alternatively that due notice is given to the government of Alberta of the banks' unwillingness to maintain these necessary services in which case we must insist that we be left free to organize our own banking system to serve the needs of our people.
William Aberhart,
Premier.
To this message I sent a reply on June 6, as follows:
Hon. William Aberhart,
Edmonton, Alberta.
I wish to acknowledge your telegram of June the 4th regarding the possible closing of branch banks throughout the province of Alberta, and to assure you that its representations are receiving the careful consideration of our government.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS

speechtext:
Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the National Parks Act and the Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island National Parks Act, 1936, to abolish the Wawaskesy national park in the province of Alberta and vest the land in the province; to change the boundaries of the Elk Island national park in the said province by adding to and parting with certain described areas and transferring the latter to the province; and to withdraw certain lands from the Prince Edward Island national park and vest the same in His Majesty in the right of the province.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this resolution is to lead up to a bill amending The National Parks Act and The Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island National Parks Act. It is necessary to make some corrections in the boundaries of the park in Prince Edward Island. As the members of the committee are aware, the gov-srnment of Prince Edward Island set aside or acquired the area that was later transferred to the dominion administration for the development of a national park in that province. This involved the acquisition of property from various individuals, and in the adjustments incidental to the acquisition of this property it is now found necessary to change in some slight particulars the boundaries of some of the areas acquired.
There is also an amendment to The National Parks Act relating to a slight change in the boundary of the Elk Island park east of Edmonton. This is a slight rectification to permit the provincial government road, which passes by the park, to take off one small corner of it, which is replaced by an addition of some thirty-five or forty acres, according to my recollection, in another part of the park.
Then there is provision for the abandonment of a park known as the Wawaskesy national park north of Medicine Hat. This was acquired quite a number of years ago for the purpose of creating a preserve for the
[Mr. Mackenzie King.l
pronghomed antelope in Alberta. It has never been fenced. It consisted of a sort of elbow in the Saskatchewan river. At the same time another park west and south of Medicine Hat, known as the Nemiskam park, was secured for the same purpose, and now it is felt that it is unnecessary to maintain both parks. A resolution was passed by the Alberta legislature, I think at its last session, to the effect that the Wawaskesy park should be either fenced or abandoned by the federal government. Since the other park which I mentioned a moment ago is quite sufficient, in the judgment of the park administration, for the maintenance of the pronghorned antelope, under this legislation it is proposed to abandon the Wawaskesy park and let it revert to the ownership of the province.
I believe that covers all the amendments proposed under this legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext: Unfortunately we could not hear very much of what was said by the minister. I was wondering if he would mention the negotiations that preceded the introduction of this resolution.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext:
The matter of adjusting the boundary of the Elk Island park has been taken up with the Alberta government; indeed the request in the first instance came from that government to make this slight correction in order to permit them to carry through a road at a certain point. At the same time, according to my recollection, they suggested that they would give us an area at another point somewhat larger than the few acres we were asked to give up. So far as the Elk Island park is concerned, this action is the result of an understanding with the Alberta government.
As to Wawaskesy park, I said a moment ago that the Alberta legislature at its last session passed a resolution to the effect that the parks administration should either abandon this park or fence it. This park includes some forty or fifty square miles in a bend of the south Saskatchewan river, with a natural boundary on two sides. There has been some

National Parks Act
slight supervision given the park, costing a few hundred dollars a year, but since we have the Nemiskam park, which is a preserve for the pronghorned antelope, it is considered unnecessary to continue the Wawaskesy park. Rather than go to the expense of fencing it and providing supervision, which would involve a considerable capital outlay and a further few thousand dollars a year thereafter, we are giving up that park. No national interest will suffer in any way, because a place has been provided where this special species of antelope may be maintained.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext:
Is the change in the
boundaries of the Prince Edward Island park in the nature of an enlargement of the park, or otherwise? I gathered from the remarks of the minister, perhaps on a former occasion, that this area had1 been acquired by the provincial government and that there had been no expropriation or expenditure directly by the dominion government in connection with the acquisition of these lands. I should like to know if my recollection is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext: Then I should like to know whether the compensation to the owners of the land included in the park has been adjusted, if that is all settled, and why the area is being either enlarged or decreased.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext:
My recollection at the
moment is that the park area is being slightly curtailed; I think I am correct in that. There are some minor adjustments in connection with the acquisition of the property, but of course that is not a matter that concerns the federal administration. All we are concerned with is whether or not the area which the provincial government is willing to turn over to us is suitable for park purposes, and the slight rectifications in the boundary that are suggested will not in any sense interfere with the utilization of the area for park purposes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext: Then with respect to the park in Alberta, was there any expenditure by the dominion in connection with either its acquisition or its maintenance; and since it is now to be abandoned to the province of Alberta is there any provision for compensation, or is it just being given back?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext:
I think I am correct in saying that there was no expenditure in con-51052-242J
nection with the acquisition of the area, which was set aside at a time when the resources of Alberta were still under the control of the federal government. The only cost involved has been a few hundred dollars per year by way of supervision. As I recall it, a settler adjacent to the area was paid a few hundred dollars a year simply to be in a position to report to the federal administration anything whioh needed reporting.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext: The Wawaskesy national park, which has just been spoken of, is in my constituency. I am familiar with the neighbourhood and I was surprised to hear that any money had been spent on it at all. I know that the land has been vacant, with the antelope either going on or off, as they see fit, in their grazing. I must say that both governments are to be commended in releasing this area from its original condition as a national park. As such it is purely a waste. Furthermore, so far as paying money to anyone for the superintendency of Wawaskesy park is concerned, I would say that such money has been wasted. I am surprised to learn that anyone has been paid, because it has been the natural place for anyone to go who wanted to hunt antelope. In my opinion, this is an excellent step.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF EXISTING LEGISLATION AFFECTING WAWASKESY, ELK ISLAND AND PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND PARKS
speechtext:
The only expenditure incurred in the past in connection with this park was approximately $200 a year, which was paid to a resident close to the park, so that if occasion arose for the making of a report to the federal parks administration someone would be on hand to do it.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT

speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved that the house go into committee of supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
house resolves itself into a committee of supply I should like again to direct the government's attention to the situation that exists in Vancouver, unless it has been modified within the last few hours. There appears to be a complete violation of any thought of law and order, or regard for it. A federal property has been at the command of a group of trespassers for between three weeks and a month. Such a thing has never been heard of before in Canada, or, so far as I know, in any other British dominion.
There is an entire and utter disregard of the provisions of the law. Public property, a post office, is under the complete control of a band of men so far as the lobby is concerned. It is useless to say there is no interference with the transaction of public business; for people cannot come and go as they have been accustomed to do by reason of the presence of these men.
I am not expressing any opinion as to whether they have a grievance or not. That is a matter to be settled at some other time. But I do protest against this complete disregard of law and order. If there is one thing this country should stand for more than another, it is the observance of law and order. And when one has regard to the wording of a poster that has been placed on a telephone pole in the city of Vancouver, having reference to the young communists and their activity in this connection, one realizes that the matter is much more serious than would appear upon the face of it.
The question is: What has this government done as the custodian for the time being of the reputation and good name of the Dominion of Canada to see that the federal property maintained by the Post Office Department of Canada has been made available for business and free from trespassers? It is not the duty of the provincial government to remove these trespassers from that property. It is not their job. The duty falls upon the people who represent the crown in the right of the dominion, and the crown in the right of the dominion is the Dominion of Canada, not the province of British Columbia. It is the bounden duty of this government to maintain law and order, to free from trespassers the property erected for a post office, and to see that the grievance is adjusted.
Certainly we must make it clear that trespassers cannot take possession of property that belongs to the people, or the crown, in the right of the dominion, and not the province or the city.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not like to have that form of presentation go without a protest. I myself have urged again and again that the dominion government should take action with regard to the situation in Vancouver. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) suggests that the men may have a grievance, but that that is not the point, and that this grievance may be settled at some other time.
I cannot think of the matter in that way, at all. If the men have a grievance, as I believe they have, now is the time to settle it. These men have resorted to extraordinary expedients in order that attention may be called to their situation. But the question is not that law and order shall come first; it is primarily whether the grievances of the men are looked after. The maintenance of "law and order" involves that justice shall be shown in the maintenance of that law and order. In my judgment, when we have hundreds of young men incapable of finding positions, we should not insist too strongly upon the maintenance of law and order as a primary consideration.
In my judgment this government has not dealt vigorously or effectively with the question. It is all very well to say that these men may go to the places from which they came. But as has been stated before in the house, most of them are not in a position to establish residence anywhere. They belong to the great army of transient workers, who have done such a great deal in the past in building up this country. As anyone who has had much to do with unemployment must know, the majority cannot readily establish residence anywhere. If they came to Winnipeg, my own city, I think in many respects they would be just as badly off, or worse off than they are in Vancouver.
We know of the situation which existed a few years ago, when the present leader of the opposition was handling the situation, and when the men came as far as Regina. What happened? Nothing much was done until there was some overt disturbance, and then action was taken. I for one do not wish to be accused of urging that these men should break the rules of law and order. They have so far maintained law and order, as that expression is generally understood. There has been no overt action. But if the government maintains its present attitude, what can be

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
expected but that one day an incident may occur which will necessitate forcible action being taken?
The leader of the opposition contends that these public buildings are federal property, that they are held by the crown in the right of the dominion, and that these men are guilty of trespass. I suggest to the leader of the opposition and to this house that the men and women of this country are worth infinitely more than our public property.
If civilization is worth anything, these men have the right to obtain a living. They are not able to obtain a living at the present time on their own initiative. What are they to do? Again and again they have appealed to this house, but in vain. I shall not discuss whether the primary responsibility lies with this parliament or with the provincial assembly. It is true that this government actually did provide projects for these men during the winter months. Under ordinary circumstances it might have been expected that with the coming of spring the men would be able to find work in building construction and so on. However, this year the situation is different. I was thinking of their case when I was out on the prairies the other day. Under normal circumstances, the farmers keep their horses and cattle under cover during the winter,. feed them, and when spring comes along put them out to graze. If that practice had been followed this year the horses and cattle would have died, because there was practically no grass on the prairies, especially in the drought areas. If they had acted on the supposition which is the basis of the attitude of the federal government, these farmers would have turned their horses and cattle out to graze as usual no matter what might have been the expected results. That has been the attitude adopted by this government.
Under normal circumstances these men would have been absorbed in the labour market, but there is little demand this year. The men can ride the freight trains and come east at the risk of being arrested or injured, as a number have been. If they get to Regina or Winnipeg they will find that things are no better. Within a block of this building we are stopped as we go to lunch by men in need of food. What would be the use of adding more men to the group already here?
Only a few days ago I received a copy of a resolution that had been passed at a meeting of the Vancouver local council of women. This reads:
Whereas: There is existing at the present time in the city of Vancouver a very serious situation in regard to the single unemployed men, and
Whereas: On several occasions the Vancouver local council of women has asked the dominion government to provide a works' scheme which would absorb these single men and thus build character, be it
Resolved: That the Vancouver local council of women reiterate its stand for a dominion public works scheme for these men, and further, be it
Resolved: That pending the implementing of such a scheme that the dominion government provide shelter and sustenance for the men.
Yours very truly,
Harriette C. Porter, Honorary Corresponding Secretary.
Personally I would rather adopt the view taken by the Vancouver local council of women than that of the leader of the opposition. I believe they are in a better position to judge the needs of these men, and their sympathies are on the right side. Boys from ordinary families are involved in this matter, and I am glad the local council has passed this resolution, which I pass on to the minister as instructed. I do hope that not many days will go by before the government realizes, to use the words of the leader of the opposition, that this situation cannot go on indefinitely. We should not wait until there is some overt act and force is necessary. In my opinion the only way to settle this matter is to provide a work and wages program.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my opinion that there is altogether too much neglect of this situation. I realize the position in which the government finds itself, but I should like to say to this house that these men are Canadians. They are the same kind of men as those who fought in the great war from 1914 to 1918. Those men were heroes when we needed them. We sang songs about when the boys would come home, and we should not forget that these men bear the same names and the same blood runs through their veins. They have been raised in the same country. They are moreover the same kind of men as those who pioneered Canada. Once in a while we hear someone say that we must have population. They will sometimes say, let us have a more active immigration policy. But what is the use of having an active immigration policy when we do not take care of the men who are here now? If we recognize that we need more people in Canada, and we surely do, we should first take care of those who are here.

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
This country should be filled by a great population. Are we never going to change the conditions in Canada so that our people can make a living? Have we reached the point of saturation with respect to population? What is happening in Canada is due to the present system. It has been the constant contention of my group that there should be a modification of our present system, as a result of which all these men could be cared for. Members can sneer about this all they want to, but they cannot sneer those men out of that post office building. They cannot sneer into employment the thousands and thousands of men in this country who are in a similar situation.
Very often those who are well fed contend that there is work for all, but the experience of these unfortunate boys is patent evidence that there is not. There are too many who believe that all the unemployed have to do is show a willingness to work. Last year I saw something which I shall never forget. I saw hundreds of these boys riding the freight trains, going from place to place. I saw them get off the trains and wander out into the far places. I saw them seeking work and willing to do anything for almost nothing. Yet they were being turned away. What are they going to do? Something must be done. We cannot have men in a position like this indefinitely. It is a disgrace to this country. There is no doubt that we are strong enough to smash them if we desire. We have our tear gas. our poison gas, our bombs, our airplanes and all the rest of it, and these men are more helpless than sheep. But the mere fact that we rely on the strength of our civilization should make us more conscious of the fact that we should initiate action and not wait until they put on the pressure which may bring about that result.
There is inadequate work in this country for the willing workers. There must be a change in our system so that people may be employed. To say that there is no work to be done in producing goods and services is to say a thing which is an utter and manifest absurdity. Why should we not make such a change as will enable these men to be absorbed? These changes could be made. All that the well-fed people do who are placed on parliament hill to take care of these men is simply to treat lightly, laugh or sneer about the whole matter, and disregard any suggestions that may be made as to a possible solution. That is all I have seen since I have been in this house. It may be believed that the old system .under which we are living will solve this

problem, but I say it will not. All the generations in the future will prove this. Why should we wait until we are forced into the ditch before we begin to build a bridge?
I was talking with a lady the other day when coming down on the train. She was a refined lady from one of the best of homes, and she was telling me something of the conditions existing out there. She says that the butchers and various suppliers of food take turns to give these boys the things they need to live on, and it must be done. Women also take turns in cooking and bringing in food for them. That indicates clearly that the citizens of Vancouver sympathize in the deepest way with these unfortunate boys, realizing that their own boys might under other circumstances be there. Hon. members can easily realize how serious conditions are if they imagine their own boys being there. It is easy for anyone with a good income sufficient to take care of his own boys not to be disturbed by the situation, but suppose one of our boys was there and we were as helpless as the fathers of these boys are to give them any employment whatever or to take care of them; we should begin to realize the gravity of our problem. If the ordinary citizens of Vancouver will make the sacrifices they are making to maintain these boys for three weeks, surely the united people of Canada, speaking and acting through this parliament, can do something to alleviate their hardships.
Hon. NORMAN McL. ROGERS (Minister of Labour):	Mr. Speaker, this question has
been before the house on a number of previous occasions. This afternoon it has been approached from three different points of view. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) would have us deal with it by means of forcible ejection.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
I did not say that. On
a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I am not going to permit the Minister of Labour any longer to misrepresent what I said. I never used the word force in the observations I made. I said the men were trespassers and that it was the duty of the government to see that this trespassing ceased.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Certainly I accept the correction of the leader of the opposition.
The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation has suggested that the situation should be met by what can only be described as submission upon the part of the government to a mass demonstration in one province looking towards the provision of

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
special works projects for a particular group of unemployed. I do not say that offensively in any way. I think it is entirely borne out by the facts.
The leader of the Social Credit group would have us meet the situation by the provision of work to relieve all those who are unemployed right across this dominion.
We as a government have had to meet this situation from the beginning with a due sense of responsibility, and we felt that we had to meet it on the basis of justifying any action we might take upon grounds of principle, and not upon grounds of mere expediency. We have proceeded upon the basis of consultation and cooperation with the provincial government. We have taken the ground that those closest to the situation were best able to advise upon it. Therefore when the Minister of Labour of British Columbia made his statement that so far as non-resident transients were concerned they should be given transportation to their homes or places of origin, we gave support to that view. The Minister of Labour in British Columbia at the same time expressed his opinion that with regard to those transients who were not non-residents but who could establish residence in British Columbia, there would be available employment for them in the next few months. Whether the Minister of Labour is correct or not in that assumption, none of us is able to say.
I would point out, however, that this situation has not now developed for the first time. Last year these camps were closed; they had in them an even greater number of men than they have had in the past season, and there was no mass demonstration in Vancouver; there was no provision of works projects to give employment to the men. This year a very considerable number of the men who were in the camps last year did not return, proving that they had either found employment elsewhere or returned to their homes on the prairies. I believe that at the present time not more than five hundred of these men who are in Vancouver are non-residents. At the beginning of the difficulty possibly the number of non-resident transients would have been in the neighbourhood of twelve hundred. That at least is the information that comes to me.
I have stated before to this house, and it must commend itself, I think, to every member, that you cannot cure this problem of transiency by creating preferred conditions for transients in any one province of the dominion. I think that must appeal to everyone as
being reasonable, upon reflection. If you establish a special position for these men, whatever justification my hon. friends have said they are willing to give them, and who have sought to obtain their ends by methods which do involve at least a breach of order-if you establish a special position for them how can you deny providing special works projects to every single group of unemployed right across this country? That has not been the policy of this government or of any other government in this country.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: That does not matter. It is time we had a change.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: This government has met that situation from the beginning, and must take and does take full responsibility for the policy that has been followed. So far as the administration of relief within the province is concerned, that is a matter which is effectively within provincial control. We have never withheld generous assistance with respect to relief to any province of this dominion.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker. I have just this to say with regard to the words of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers). Members from the city of Vancouver have endeavoured in every way possible to bring the gravity of the situation home to the minister, and his statements in this house, in which he takes refuge, are the strongest indictment that could be brought of the most cruel and callous indifference of the government to the most serious distress. The men were released en masse a few months ago without adequate means for their support.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Not en masse.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
In rotation. The last deferred pay vouchers that were given to a comparatively small group of these men were distributed on May 15, and they have been absolutely without means since. They were compelled to organize for their mutual benefit-something they had a perfect right to do.
The minister refers to conditions of last year. The conditions this spring were entirely different. There was no demonstration last year because there was some work available. At the present time plants and subsidiary operations are closing down. Yesterday the Woodfibre and Port Alice plants closed down, which every year absorb a large number of men, and all operations connected with these plants are at a standstill. The Powell river pulp and paper plant, that tremendous plant, is working only half time, and all related bush operations are slack.

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
I am going to tell the minister now that the real cause of the trouble is that he has an incompetent officer on the job in Vancouver. One good man representing the federal government would have settled this matter weeks ago. He is being badly advised. Read the editorials in the Vancouver papers and the resolutions that have been passed by different bodies of the citizens of Vancouver. The member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has referred to the resolution of the local council of women, which resolution must have reached the minister. Resolutions have been received by him from responsible bodies of citizens who have no friendly alliance with the communist party, on which the minister places all the blame for this situation. I have a resolution from Reverend Father Cooper, than whom none is more outstanding for his devoted and unselfish service on behalf of the underprivileged. This resolution was signed by Archbishop DePencier, of the diocese of New Westminster. These men in their considered judgment all say that the correct remedy is to provide employment for these men. It is not a question of the government submitting to mass demonstration. Mark you, these men who are unemployed in Vancouver went prior to the demonstration in an orderly, helpful and lawful way to the authorities asking for consideration of their special needs this spring, and were denied consideration of their needs or any proper consideration of their problems. It was only when municipalities all across the country had been wired to, and the men found that there was no work for them elsewhere, that they resorted to this spectacular means of demonstrating their needs. One good man with some authority to deal with the situation could devise a plan, with perhaps a little face-saving on both sides, and a little understanding of the problem, which would end the trouble. The problem could be dissipated overnight; but for the minister to sit here and say that nothing will be done, and take refuge behind official red tape, can only provoke trouble in this situation.
Why does the minister suppose nothing has been done? Colonel Foster, the chief of police of Vancouver, is a cool-headed man. and many times the citizens of Vancouver have been thankful that at the head of the police administration we have had a cool-headed man. He has ample force at his command. He has at his call the provincial police reserves. It would be a comparatively easy matter to toss tear gas bombs into the Post Office and art gallery. Why does be not do it? He knows that the art gallery, in which have been stored irreplaceable art [Mr. MacNedt.1
treasures which mean a great deal to the people of Vancouver and to the cultural development of that city, would be ruined in a few minutes by the attempts of the men to escape. Have you ever seen a mob of men try to escape from the effects of tear gas, as I have seen them, not once, but several times in Vancouver? Incalculable damage would be done, and there is always the danger of loss of life. Force is not being applied because the citizens of Vancouver are well aware that the men have a legitimate grievance. They know that there is not work available for them, and it is the definite responsibility of the minister to present in direct negotiation with the men some plan which will disclose to them avenues of employment, so that they shall not be thrown out by force into a situation which confronts them with nothing but blank hopelessness.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I doubt if there is anything more that we can do here to get action from this government. We have appealed to them from every point of view, I think, from which an appeal can be made. I wish to confirm what has already been said by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil). In my opinion you may wear these men out, but the possibilities are that by the time you have worn them out they will be prepared for anything, and then we are going to have trouble, and trouble that could have been avoided by compromise and good-will on both sides. If a compromise were offered by this government or its representatives I am satisfied that the men would meet them more than half way.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me? Has he seen-I assume he has- a copy of the telegram which I sent to Mr. Matts, the secretary of the committee, in which it was made clear to him that, either in British Columbia or in any other province, these men would not be disqualified in any way, would be equally eligible with others in the same position for youth training plans or for any other public works which might be available ?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
What does that
mean?

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
It means as much as it
ever meant.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
That does not mean anything to a hungry man. What the Minister of Labour says to these men is, "You may be hungry to-day, and we are not going to do anything about it, but if you move out of here and go on being hungry, we won't hold it against you six months from now."

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
That is not good enough, and I do not think if the minister were hungry he would accept what he said to-day as being good enough. Perhaps the provincial government will do something for the unemployed two or three or four months hence. It may be that the provincial government will do something then; but again, it may be that the provincial government will not, until they get federal assistance. The city of Vancouver to-day is carrying 2,500 men more than it was carrying this time last year, because of the shifting of the burden on to the city by the federal and the provincial authorities. Let me tell the minister that that was not the basis on which this government went to the country in 1935. That was not what was promised the unemployed by the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the city of Vancouver. That was not what was promised the unemployed by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) in the city of Vancouver time and time again. All that these men are asking is that the government fulfil its promises and provide work. And let me say again that they are not very particular; the wages they have been working for have not been very high.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
They worked hard last
year.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: They worked hard; and if the government has nothing more than the excuses which have been offered by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) in the last six weeks, all I can say is that this government is bankrupt indeed, and will pay the price of that bankruptcy some day in the. near future.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
It appears to me that the minister views the situation as being temporary, that he thinks that unemployment is a temporary condition; so he suggests that the unemployed leave the province of British Columbia and go back to the locality from which they came, and when they arrive there the federal government will assist the province in providing employment or some measure of relief for them. But I do not believe that the government has assured these men that if they do go back to the locality from which they came, work will be provided for them. Can the minister tell the house whether that is so? Has the promise of work ever been made to these men provided they go back to the point from which they originally came?
Reference has been made to the promises of the Liberal party, one of which was that they would issue money and credit to meet
the needs of the people of Canada. The unemployed in Vancouver, in common with the unemployed throughout Canada, are in need of purchasing power so that they may be able to provide for their basic needs. They want to have a place to sleep and something to eat. This is an emergency situation. If war were to break out, that also, would be an emergency situation, but the government could then find the money to provide the men with food, clothing and shelter, and possibly give them $1.10 per day. If unemployment is a temporary condition, if the minister thinks that Liberal policies are going to provide the citizens of this country with the opportunity to work, surely during this emergency he can provide them with at least $1.10 per day. I am sure that in that event the men will vacate the premises they occupy at the present time. I do not believe they want to create any difficulty. They are taking this action solely with a view of bringing to the attention of Canada their legitimate claims. They have a just grievance. I believe if the minister offered them employment in the areas from which they come he would have no further difficulty with them.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: I should like to add my views to those of my leader in his protest against the conditions under which these men are compelled to exist. I was struck by one word used by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), namely the word "submission," his remark that he hates to submit to the dictates of unemployed men. I sometimes think that we in this house have lost all sense of democracy.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: The hon. member never had it.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
Let me say that we have the duty of satisfying the demands of the public. That is what we are here for, not to dictate and to tell them what they cannot have, but to supply their needs. This is not a new condition. Not only during the term of office of this government but while the last government was in power, excuses were made. They passed the word from the federal government to the provincial government, from the provincial government back to the municipalities; and now, after seven or eight long years, we find these conditions still existing. Are we to have another Regina incident? Or are we big enough to get down and reason these things out on the right basis? Is there work in this country? Have we the money to put these men to work? Can we use the national credit and all the instruments we have at our disposal to give these men employment and create national assets? Those

Unemployed Men in Vancouver
are the important questions. Anything which happens in Vancouver will not be the responsibility of the men who at the present time are occupying a public building; it will be the responsibility of this government.
We are not dealing with units; we are dealing with human beings. For seven years we have continually carried out the policy to which this leads, destroying men's souls, taking the best that is in men and destroying it, because being stiffnecked we make these men political footballs-" We are not going to give way to the dictates of provincial governments," and all that kind of thing. We should not in this house, on these questions, speak as social crediters or Liberals, we should speak as Canadians and as representatives of the people. If we are going to do anything to bring about a new feeling of confidence in this country I do not think there is any better place to begin than in the city of Vancouver by providing these men with employment. If this government has to bend a little, if it has to give way to what has been described as " demands," what does it matter? The essential thing is, let us get results. We have money for all kinds of purposes less deserving than the unemployed situation. I ask the Minister of Labour: Could not the government within twenty-four hours, if they were determined to do so, put these men to work? They could do it if they made up their mind that these men were going to work in a fair way; why then will they not do it? What are they waiting for.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Twenty-five dollars a month.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Well, that remark is stupid nonsense, and it is time to cut iit out. This question is too serious for this shouting across the floor " $25 a month " every time I rise to speak. We are dealing with the unemployment problem facing the youth of this country, youth, the finest asset any nation has. It is your job to make your contribution and see that these men get a break.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext: Ask him what solution he has to offer.

maintopic: UNEMPLOYMENT-CONCENTRATION OF SINGLE UNEMPLOYED MEN IN VANCOUVER- STATEMENT OF MR. BENNETT
speechtext:
This excuse about transients and non-residents has been used on so many occasions. "Send these people back to where they came from." I do not care if they came from Halifax; they are Canadian citizens, that is all that matters. We should treat them all on an equal basis, not say to them: Go back to Halifax, and we will do something for you there. People know by this time that that is only a way of passing the buck, of evading responsibility. I do not think the minister

is lacking in humanitarian feeling; I know he is not. I have a high regard for him, but I should like to see him do something now about this situation. Do not let us have another disgraceful incident such as we had in Regina, where men were clubbed down; that leaves only bitterness and disunity and division when we should be giving the world a lead in national unity and reasonable understanding. getting together and discussing common problems. There is no use in letting a situation like this develop. I appeal to the government, joining my voice with the voices of my colleagues who have spoken this afternoon. There is no more serious question before the house at this time than this Vancouver situation. Put these boys to work and you will find that communism and radicalism will pass away like mists before the morning sun.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I have another matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the house. It concerns the Canadian National railway and an attempted use of it for political purposes by Liberal officials in some parts of Canada.
I have in my hand a notice which was sent out through the regular roadmaster's channels on the Margo subdivision of the Canadian National railways just prior to the provincial election in Saskatchewan last week. I hold in my hand new form 171, dated at Kam-sack, Saskatchewan, June 6, 1938. It reads:
To Section Foremen and Section Labourers
The Liberal government is very strongly against amalgamation with the C.P.R. If the Saskatchewan Liberal government is defeated in this election we will get amalgamation very soon, trains will be taken off and branch lines, many of them, will be closed. All Canadian National employees should vote Liberal.
"Liberal" is underlined with red ink.
See that your wives and as many of your friends as possible vote Liberal.
Attached to that is "A plain talk to railway workers" published by authority of the Saskatchewan Liberal Association, Regina, Saskatchewan. The "plain talk" reads:
A railwayman who has a job is a useful citizen of the community. He has his pay cheque, his community interest, he looks after his family, he puts something aside for his later years.
A railwayman out of a job is just another one of the unemployed. He becomes a problem to himself and to the community.

Saskatchewan Election
Those who would merge or amalgamate the two railway systems of Canada are more interested in things than in human beings. They may say that they are working to save the taxpayer but they overlook the fact that the railway worker is one of the best taxpayers in Canada.
The railways of Canada and the railway workers of Canada are needed to carry on the business of the country. Given a ten per cent upturn in business the railways will be able to get along. They will be needed.
In a large, richly-endowed country like Canada that ten per cent increase is sure to come. In the meantime the railways may do something to help themselves by minor adjustments.
A railway monopoly, whatever it might be for the country, will be of no value to the railway workers. The workers will be in the hands of the monopoly.
The Liberal party is the one party that has stood firmly against amalgamation. It stands there to-day.
Numerous leaders of the Conservative party are working for amalgamation of the Canadian railways. Read the speeches of Senator Meighen and others.
The C.C.F. would "socialize" the railways, creating a monopoly. It would be referred to as a publicly-owned enterprise but it would still be a monopoly.
Social credit has no railway policy. It works on the theory that if enough money is printed by printing presses, as handbills are printed, the railway problem would look after itself.
The Liberal party is the safe party for the railway workers. The Liberal party has never wavered as to the rights of the railway worker. Saskatchewan railway workers can show by voting Liberal that Saskatchewan wants no amalgamation.
Vote Liberal.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Now, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal benches applaud. If this kind of letter, sent out by roadmasters to the railway workers of Saskatchewan, containing this leaflet, is sent out by a national railway official, he should be subjected to the severest criticism and to discipline.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Who sent the first letter out?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: I have given particulars, and I can provide the name.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Who sent the first one?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: I will tell you in a few moments.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Why not tell it now?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
I say further that there is no group in this house which stands as unitedly as the group with which I am
associated against railway amalgamation or unification, and people throughout the country know that.
I have here the letter, dated June 9, received by me to-day, which accompanied the communication I have just read. It is from Mr. A. M. Nicholson. I quote:
The enclosed was handed to me just before a meeting at Canora on June 7. It was received by a C.N.R. employee who prefers not to have his name known.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: The reason for the omission of the name is quite obvious; anyone who knows anything about that Saskatchewan Liberal machine knows that it intimidates large numbers of workers and relief recipients in that province.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: That is not true.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
The letter continues:
Three other employees came to me after the meeting and had similar communications. The employees are Ukrainians who had intended voting C.C.F. but who were greatly disturbed by the contents of this message on company stationery, and also by the fact that it was delivered through C.N.R. mail in the road-master's envelope.
Will you please do what you can to see that whoever has been responsible for intimidating voters in this manner is properly dealt with.
This occurred on the Margo subdivision of the Canadian National railways. I shall be glad to supply any necessary affidavits. Will you please return by registered mail.
That is signed by Mr. Nicholson. A moment ago I was asked who signed the original letter. The writer had not the nerve to sign his name to it, but it is so easily traceable that, now that it is brought to the attention of the Minister of Transport, there will be no difficulty in finding out who sent it. I had not seen one of these letters, Mr. Speaker; I had heard of similar communications in other parts of the province, though I could not lay my hands on them. This came to me, without having been requested, by registered mail this morning.
As a believer in public ownership, I stand for our publicly owned institutions; yet when attempts to use them are made by political parties or officials interested in the success of political parties for partisan ends, then I say it is time this house sat up and took notice of the situation. This is the rankest kind of intimidation. A few moments ago we heard speakers from several quarters of this house discuss the situation at Vancouver, where men are jobless. These in Saskatchewan, humble railway workers, some
Saskatchewan Election

of them with families, receive a communication of this description and are intimidated; they are made to fear that if certain things happen they will be in the bread line, and I say that in a British democracy any group of people who dare use the bread of our fellow citizens in order to take from them their full rights of citizenship and franchise ought to be condemned in the eyes of every decent citizen of this country.
I rise in my place this afternoon because I have been associated with elections in Saskatchewan for a very long time, and I have seen this sort of thing go on year after year, with teachers afraid to express themselves because it was so worked that the boards would get rid of them if they did; with ministers of the gospel moved from place to place if they expressed an opinion against the most unscrupulous political machine you can find in north America. What we have heard this afternoon is the sort of thing that should be frowned upon by every citizen. From time to time I have quoted in this house from Escott Reid's article in the Political Science Quarterly of February, 1935, wherein he outlines the methods under which the Saskatchewan Liberal machine has operated in days gone by. We know that whenever movements arise in western Canada that seek to unite the people, that machine is able to intimidate and divide. It was the attorney general of Saskatchewan who, in regard to social credit, confessed, "We started a prairie fire. Now we have to put it out." We know what that phrase meant. We know how some of these social credit candidates came into Saskatchewan in 1935, into some of the constituencies which we represent. We know the whole story, and in bringing this matter to the attention of the house this afternoon I have in mind not only this sort of intimidation but also the reference made by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Poole), a few moments ago to the situation that occurred in the city of Regina in 1935.
When men are jobless they are desperate; and if they are threatened with the loss of their jobs they become desperate also. I say a threat of this description is something of which we should take notice. I was in Regina just three years ago, almost three years to the day. I saw those seventeen hundred boys arrive there. I mingled with them that evening; over the air I appealed to citizens to assist them. I moved among them and found them peaceful, law-abiding boys. I believe the government at Ottawa was misinformed regarding the situation there, and day by day I saw those boys become 
more restless. Just a day or so before the riots occurred I was among them, and they told me there was no need to worry. I had done what I could for them; I advised them to obey the law and maintain order, and then the riots occurred. I do not want to see a repetition of that in Vancouver, in Regina, in Calgary, in Winnipeg, or in any other city of Canada. But that is the sort of thing that is brought about when you take from the people the right to express themselves at the polls. Then you leave them only one alternative, an alternative to which I am absolutely opposed; but matters such as we have discussed this afternoon make it more difficult all the time for those of us who believe in democracy to maintain and propagate it for the achievement of orderly progress.
So I am bringing to the attention of the government and this house this communication, which is easily traceable, in order that steps may be taken to see that the person responsible for this sort of thing may be properly disciplined. In the future I believe conduct of this sort should be punishable not by fine but by imprisonment, and by a fairly steep sentence at that.

speechtext: The election in Saskatchewan is over, and I do not see that much good can be served by fighting it over again in this House of Commons when we have more important matters to attend to, but that is what the representations made this afternoon amount to.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: May I ask whether the Prime Minister is averse to having this matter investigated by the government or the Minister of Transport?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: I have been sitating that the Canadian National railways is a body that is supposed to be independent of government control, and the government should not interfere one way or the other in this matter unless, after the Canadian National authorities have investigated, they communicate to us their need of government assistance in order that rules and regulations may be enforced.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have had the amazing spectacle to-day of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) trying to drag the Canadian National railways into partisan politics in this house.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: I object.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: And this on the unsupported word of a hired socialist organizer who left the preaching of the gospel to engage in partisan politics.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. I am referring to a document sent out through the regular railway channels and dated at Kamsack.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: If the hon. member would give me a minute, I would come to that phase of it. At the very outset, the complaint that has been made before this house to-day should not have been made here. It is that either someone used Canadian National stationery for improper purposes, or that someone improperly used the Canadian National name in printing stationery for his own purposes.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Or the Liberal leaflet attached.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: I never knew there was a law against sending out Liberal propaganda in this country. The leaflet in itself was perfectly all right. It was truthful, moderate, reasonable and constructive. My hon. friend said a moment ago that he and his party were opposed to amalgamation. I can get the original handbook distributed by the hon. member, either by himself or by his agent in a meeting which he was addressing, in which he said the object of his party was to socialize the natural resources of this country, and the implements of production and means of transportation.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
What has that to do with
this?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Let me ask this: How can you socialize public ownership? How can you socialize the transportation system of this country without having a monopoly? Would you with one hand administer the Canadian National Railways, with the other hand administer the Canadian Pacific railway, and depend on your feet to administer the other means of transportation?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Does the hon. member wish me to answer that point?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
My hon. friend has said that people have been losing their jobs because of political pressure being brought to bear on them. I would tell him that in my observation more men have lost their jobs or had to change their locations because of pressure brought by his socialist friends than I have seen affected by the democratic parties. A complaint of this nature should not have been made. Everyone in this house,
Saskatchewan Election

who has had anything to do with public business, knows that Canadian National business is dealt with in another manner. It is dealt with by a special committee of the house, which considers the accounts of the company, and officers of the company appear before the committee. It might be quite true that the hon. member does not believe in these men on the Canadian National railways being encouraged to express their own opinions about amalgamation, or more socialization than there is at the present time. I think the hon. member would agree with me in saying that the only wrong that has been done in this case is either the using of the stationery of the railway, the misusing of the company name, or the enclosing of political statements in company mail. If one of these things has been done, it certainly can be investigated by the company.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the point at issue has escaped the attention of both the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). The point is this: Here is a document alleged- and I use the word advisedly-to have been sent out by an officer of the Canadian National Railways.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Alleged by whom?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Just a moment. The
document is on the stationery of the Canadian National Railways, new form, No. 171. It is typical railway stationery and appears to be quite genuine. The document is dated at Kamsack, Saskatchewan, June 6, 1938, which would indicate the source from which it was issued. That would aid in the investigation of the matter, should the government desire to investigate it.
Now, nothing can be said against the Liberal party or any other party expressing its views in connection with governing this country on railway or other matters. If the Liberal party, as indicated this afternoon by the applause of its members in the house, are opposed to unification and amalgamation, that is their privilege. They have a perfect right so to advocate. But when Canadian National Railways stationery is used, or appears to have been used, and sent out by an official of the railway, as the evidence would indicate, and when on it one finds language in these words: "The Liberal government is very strongly against amalgamation with the C.P.R.", I suggest the matter should be considered. Then, I ask the Prime Minister to note this particularly:
If the Saskatchewan Liberal government is defeated in this election, we will get amalgama-

tion very soon, trains will be taken off and branch lines many of them will be closed. All Canadian National employees should vote Liberal.
That is what I think is the serious point in the matter. It all depends upon whether the document is as it appears to be.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
Just a minute; I will
come to that, if hon members will be patient. The point in the matter is this: If Canadian National officials, by virtue of their office and influence with employees and workers on the railway, are permitted to use Canadian National stationery to make declarations which, if not untrue, are obviously not based upon any authority, then I say it is a very serious matter. That is the sort of thing that drags the Canadian National into politics. My opinion during the years I have been in the house-and I think it is shared pretty generally by hon. members on both sides-is that it is highly desirable to keep the Canadian National Railways out of politics, if we can. I say, "if we can", because the experience over a long period of years would indicate that it is an extremely difficult thing to do. I think no one can say that we should not make every endeavour to do so.
A moment ago the Prime Minister suggested that the complaint should have been addressed to the president of the Canadian National Railways. I differ from him, and I say that this is the proper place in which to discuss a matter of this kind.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: An anonymous letter?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: My suggestion is that the Prime Minister represents the government of the country, and he ought to draw the attention of the president of the railways to it, and request that the whole matter be investigated by a competent officer of the company.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: An anonymous letter?

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: It is not an anonymous letter.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: Surely it is.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: I asked the hon. member to let me have this document.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
If the chief whip of the Liberal party would permit me, I should like to proceed. Any citizen of Canada is at liberty, through a member, to bring to the attention of the House of Commons any

grievance, and particularly at this point, on going into supply. He may mention any grievance to which he or others may be subjected.
I am not vouching for this, because I do not know the man. I simply say that the evidence of the stationery warrants that the matter be investigated.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
No, there is no signature. I suggest that that is quibbling, if I may be permitted to use the term without offence. It is rather begging the question. I submit to the Prime Minister that with this stationery before us, and with a responsible citizen, whatever his views may be, bringing it to the attention	of	parliament	through the properchannel, namely through a member of the House of Commons, the Prime Minister and the government owe it to the house and to the hon.	member who	brought it to	theattention	of	the house	to investigate	the
matter. I would not condemn the Liberal party or anyone else on this evidence until it has been investigated.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext: It is not evidence at all.

maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) says it is not evidence, but I submit that though it may not be sufficient to condemn, it is sufficient to warrant investigation. That is the point I make. I submit	to	the Prime	Minister that	the
matter should be investigated carefully at the instance of the government. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar or myself or anyone else has not the right to request the president of the railway to do anything, but the government has the right, particularly where it is alleged-I use the word advisedly-that officers of the railway have projected themselves into a political controversy and have used influences which they were not justified in using. In my opinion that is the point at issue.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SASKATCHEWAN ELECTION-ALLEGED USE OP CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FOR POLITICAL PURPOSES-STATEMENT OF MR. COLDWELL
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend that if instead of the Canadian National Railways being involved, this particular incident had had to do with some high official of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, that he had used stationery belonging to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to accompany an anonymous circular and have it distributed at the instance of the employees of the Canadian
Pacific Railway Company, would he not assume that the president and the board of directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would take cognizance of a matter of the kind? The position of the government with respect to the Canadian National Railways is that the Canadian National stands on all fours, so far as freedom from government interference is concerned, with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Assurance has been given the president and the board of directors that if in investigating this matter themselves they should require the assistance of the government, that assistance will be given in the fullest measure. I think myself it is the duty of the higher officers of the railway concerned to investigate matters of the kind, whether they have to do with the government owned or the privately owned railway. I do not think it is the business of the government to be continually telling both railway companies what they should do with respect to their officials and employees.

I told him then that this question might be answered more appropriately when we were dealing with the item having to do with training projects for unemployed young people, but that I would try to supply the information while the present item was under discussion.

In some provinces, particularly Ontario, the selection of trainees for different projects was made by officials of the employment offices, but in most provinces the employment offices were not used in that capacity. The women's section of the employment service gave valuable assistance in .helping to select young women for home service training schools and in their subsequent placement in employment. The facilities of all employment offices were available to trainees on the completion of their

course to assist them in finding employment. With respect to the other training plans carried on during the past year, it is suggested that the connection is a valuable one and ought to be improved further by the appointment of a number of special placement officers in the provinces where these plans are being carried out.

Could the minister state how many of the men now in the Vancouver post office and art gallery would be eligible for forestry training? I understand that the forestry training camps were opened again last week and that some hundreds of young men from British Columbia have been sent lo these camps.

I have not that information before me, but I shall be glad to get it for my hon. friend when the item which refers more specifically to the matter is under discussion.
The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) asked a question with regard to the follow-up facilities of the employment service in connection with the placing of domestic help. I may say that when this matter was brought to the attention of the committee last year by my hon. friend I arranged for the director of the employment service to speak directly with him in order to secure specific complaints. My information is that at that time my hon. friend did not supply any specific information which would have enabled an investigation to be made. Later on he made it clear that he had Vancouver in mind, and a telegram was sent to Mr. McVety, the superintendent of the Employment Service of Canada in British Columbia. The text of Mr. McVety's reply is as follows:
Only one ease in twenty years where employment service has received unfavourable criticism and this was in May, 1934. Girl twenty-one years of age, sent as domestic to residence in good district, was accompanied by a married woman with whom she was living who inspected home and advised girl to take position. Home later turned out to be operated by procurers who were sent to prison for various terms. Position of department in matter fully investigated by minister-
That is the minister of labour for British Columbiaand local council of women who agreed every precaution had been taken. Vancouver city police prosecutor who made_ investigation and handled prosecution in preliminary hearing quite satisfied no blame attached to department and expressed thanks for assistance in obtaining witnesses. If Mr. MacNeil has any other case in mind will be glad to have particulars.

As my hon. friend is aware, it is very difficult to follow up these cases unless specific complaints are made. I can assure him that if he has any particular case in mind I shall be only too glad to investigate it for him.

I wish to assure the minister that neither at this time nor last year was I attempting to single out the Vancouver office for criticism, nor was I suggesting that they were conniving to bring about circumstances which would be to the disadvantage of these single homeless girls. I advocate, and I hope the minister will encourage, the development of facilities that will afford every precaution. I hesitate to bring specific cases to the attention of the department or to introduce them into a public discussion. There is no doubt that sometimes young girls in destitute circumstances are exploited by unscrupulous persons. They are asked to work at low wages or to do work that is too arduous. Advantage is deliberately taken of their unfortunate circumstances. Frequently they have been exposed to the operations of procurers for the chain of brothels in the interior of British Columbia. I am not criticizing the Vancouver office. I am urging the federal government to give them every cooperation in extending the follow-up facilities. I believe it would be the desire of the officials in charge of the women's division of the Vancouver employment service to develop those facilities as far as possible, and I urge that some definite plan be adopted so that these transient young women, who are frequently in a helpless condition when they reach Vancouver, shall be given every assistance and protection.

I can assure my hon. friend that that certainly is the desire of those who direct the employment service, and some indication that the service is operated reasonably well in that respect is that very few complaints have been received. Certainly as soon as any are received they will be investigated.
Will the minister develop the follow-up facilities?
Yes, I shall do whatever can be done in that direction.
