There is another matter. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) is not here, and I was desirous of obtaining certain information. When the minister was absent from the department the Minister of Labour was acting Minister of National Defence, and in view of what took place in this house the other day I have now authentic and much more complete information than I had when I was speaking then. The first question I desire to ask is this: Did the administrating officer at the Royal Military College make a report, which was entered in the R.M.C. central registry in May, 1937, and which was communicated here, and did the minister himself as acting Minister of National Defence make a reply to that document?

I will answer at once that I have no recollection at the present time of that report having been brought to my attention or of a reply having been made, but I shall attempt to ascertain if that was the case.

I will help the minister
with respect to it. At noon on the second day of January, 1937, Major Stethem, now Lieutenant-Colonel Stethem, retired administrating officer of the Royal Military College, was proceeding to his home when he saw a large two-ton truck, No. 33511C, bearing the name of Louis Drinka, loading up and carting away a full load of crushed stone from the Royal Military College government stone pile near Navy bay. This pile had been diminishing in size and there had been discussions about it. As administrating officer Major Stethem followed the stone through the city and saw the truck proceed to a laneway, running west from Sydenham street. The stone was dumped into a shed in the rear of a house said to be owned or rented by Mr. Stansbury. The shed was being converted into a garage. Stethem asked the driver what authority he had for taking the government stone, and he stated he got his orders from Mr. Stansbury.
Stethem reported the matter in consequence of certain threats and matters of that sort which took place afterwards in respect to himself. The further taking of the stone was stopped; but in consequence of what happened, on the first day of May Stethem requested that his original report be a matter of record in the R.M.C. central registry.
I wonder if the minister will be good enough to look at the files of the acting minister of National Defence, where I believe he will find a reply to that report. In view of the

I suggest that the item stand until we get that information, and that the minister proceed with other items, because when I deal with this I should like to deal with it completely and fully.

Most certainly I shall
have no hesitation at all in letting the item stand until that information is brought down. But there is nothing in the report read by the leader of the opposition which in the slightest degree is at variance with the statement I made to the committee some time ago, that Mr. Stansbury himself acknowledged that he had received a load of this crushed rock with the consent of the officer in charge and that he laid that crushed rock upon places on the roadway leading to his garage. He denied vigorously the statement made by the leader of the opposition that his garage had been built with public property.

The observations I made are completely at variance with the statement made by the minister. The minister himself states that Mr. Stansbury said that he had permission to do what he did. As a matter of fact such is not the case, so far as I have been able to ascertain, for the simple reason that on the report being made by Stethem to his commanding officer, the adjutant, steps were immediately taken by telephone and further removal of the stone was stopped. The stone was quarried by government relief labour, taken to the crusher, and the operation was paid for entirely out of government funds. In consequence of what was said in the house the other day, this information has become available from the one source from which it could come and be authentic, and that is why I ask the minister to look at the files and see this report and ascertain what reply he himself sent to the Royal Military College as to what action was to be taken in the matter. A copy of his letter in any event is available at the office. The original, of course, is at the Royal Military College. That is the position at the moment.

At the time he was in the public employ, and when he came back he was given the same job again, it
[Mr. Bennett.l
having been held down during his absence by his father. He has since been convicted of a more serious offence, which involves punishment for just a day under two years,

There is another matter which I think I should mention, although the minister who referred to it is not at present in the chamber. This question in connection with coal is not at all a new matter. To my surprise I found that it was the subject matter of public discussion at the last election, and Mr. Sowards,, who has been attacked in this house, publicly said to his opponent, "I will put up a thousand dollars; you will put up a thousand dollars; I will name an engineer; you will name an engineer; they will choose a competent arbitrator; and if the bins to which you refer do not hold the amount of coal for which charges have been made. I forfeit my thousand dollars and am liable to any other penalties that may accrue to me by reason of it." That offer is still open. What is more, I have the measurements of the so-called bin. If the minister will read the solemn declaration of Mr. Gibson he will find that it does not touch this point at all. The cubical contents of the so-called bin are here, and I will give them, in view of the fact that although the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) dealt with this, and not the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers), the Minister of Labour says he is responsible for procuring the statutory declaration. The bin was 31 feet, 6 inches long, 11 feet, 9 inches wide, and 6 feet, 9 inches high, which makes a total of 2,498 cubic feet. The number of tons it will hold depends upon the kind of coal that is used, but in any event at all times that number of cubic feet would hold more than is charged for in the ledger account which has been sent to me.
There is another point with respect to that. This matter has been discussed fully on the hustings and elsewhere. The offer Mr. Sowards made is still outstanding. His opponent has never taken it up. Mr. Sowards not having access to the public buildings, I understand some changes have been made in them since then. That, however, is not a matter of great importance, because it is well to understand the kind of bins they were. They were bins with holes in the outside through which coal was dumped; there was a central opening

out of which part of the coal ran until it was thrown back in the bin, and there was a fire hole to which coal was delivered to obviate the necessity of carrying it from the storage bin to the place where it was used. The question as to the quantity of fuel used by the school, that is the public building, is not a matter over which Mr. Sowards had control. The deliveries were checked as to weights and other relevant matters, and if the government desires, although it is not their property, although it is purely a local matter and the other instances were purely provincial and not federal matters, if an honest opportunity is offered for the measurement of the bin and the determination of its capacity he will be only too glad to deal with it. We obviously as a federal power have nothing to do with it except as it was utilized by Mr. Gibson, who is a provincial and not a federal employee, who is dealing with a provincial and not a federal matter, and whose declaration, it will be observed at once, leads nowhere as far as this matter is concerned.
I was unable at first to understand why the Minister of National Defence made the statement in view of what he said the other evening; but when the Minister of Labour made the observations he dad as to his part in it, I then quite understood, and this endeavour to think that an answer is made to the question of the administration of the Labour department's office in Kingston by making that declaration against John Sowards is, I think, somewhat beside the point. Mr. Sowards is ready and willing to meet the Minister of National Defence or anybody else, but obviously he cannot meet him with respect to provincial matters. And it is an odd thing that he had no complaint in this respect from the provincial authorities, but that^ the first intimation of it, so far as any official act is concerned, came from the federal authorities, here. I need hardly say that the matter was so discussed, according to the public press, in Kingston during the last election that it became known apparently to everybody. But no action seems to have been taken by the people concerned, namely the provincial government. speechtext:
Mr. J.S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre) moved the second reading of Bill No. 119, respecting divorce and matrimonial
causes.
He said: As the house will recognize, this is a senate bill. It came over to this house and remained on the order paper for several days, and, I take it, would have been dropped had I not sponsored it.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext: Let it drop.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext:
No. I have taken it up because I believe it is highly desirable legislation. I could have wished that someone else had undertaken to pilot it through the house. However, it seemed that no one else was willing to do this, so I felt it was my responsibility because I believe this legislation should pass. Personally I have no very special interest in divorce as such. Several years ago I sponsored a bill providing for the setting up of divorce courts in Ontario. I did so simply because as one member of the house I was utterly weary of going through the performance that we do go through in passing divorce bills. Every hon. member I think recognizes the procedure: The bill is introduced in the senate; the case is investigated by a senate committee, which perhaps is not strictly in the nature of a court-members coming in and going out again in the course of the hearing-and after that it comes to us. We
have a private bills committee which gives scant attention to these cases, unless, indeed, there is some special lobby, and then we may consider the case to a certain extent. But we rarely have witnesses before us; as a rule we rely almost entirely on the printed evidence as it comes to us from the senate committee. Then, when the bills come over to this house, they are frequently passed, as they were to-night, en bloc. None of us, I fancy, knows anything as to the merits of the bills which we passed a few minutes ago. None of us knows anything much about them. We give them readings in this house, first, second and third, in a purely formal way. That procedure is not at all satisfactory. Indeed, I agree very largely with what was said the other day by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) to the effect that it is rather a scandalous procedure.
The trouble a few years ago was that we were getting large numbers of divorce cases from Ontario; indeed, it had become an open scandal, and it was for that reason that I sponsored the bill which had come from the senate providing for the setting up of a divorce court for Ontario. I believe that is the right way to handle the question of divorce. That bill did not include Quebec because of the very strong feeling against divorce which prevails in a certain section of that province. However, I think a majority of hon. members in this house will agree that the setting up of a divorce court for Ontario was the right thing to do. Certainly by this time this house would have been deluged with literally hundreds of cases, to which it could have given very little attention.
This new measure has been, as it were, laid at my door.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, the legislation in respect to Ontario has multiplied the number of divorces in that province ten times.

Perhaps it has. But let me point out to my right hon. friend that before that legislation was enacted it took a considerable amount of money to see a divorce case through parliament. Therefore only people who had money to spend to come to Ottawa and to employ lawyers could secure a divorce. My idea of justice is that it ought to be just as possible for poor people as for wealthy people to secure relief; and if people at Windsor or Niagara Falls or anywhere found it impossible to secure divorce solely for the reason that they could not come to Ottawa and employ lawyers, I think it is right that courts should be established within their reach.

speechtext: The condition is no better to-day in the courts so far as fees go than it was when divorces came before parliament.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext:
I do not see how it can be worse! I do not want anyone to state here that I am out to break up the home. I am just as anxious to preserve the home as any hon. member in this house. This measure deals only with cases in which a home is already broken. Further, I do not want anyone to say that I desire to encourage immorality. I firmly believe that this measure, if carried, will save many from temptation to immorality. Perhaps I may be permitted to say that I speak as a child of a happy home. I speak as the father and husband in a happy family. I am supported in this measure which I am advocating by a large number of people of the very highest character. Hence I hope that, whatever the nature of the debate that may follow upon the introduction of this bill, no one will begin to sling mud and suggest that there are any other than the highest motives on the part of those who favour this bill.
I speak also as a social worker who knows something of the broken homes, and would seek if possible to save something from the wreckage.
To adultery as a ground for divorce this bill would add desertion, cruelty and insanity. The bill is an adaptation of the act passed in the British House of Commons in 1937. The British act was passed on the report of a royal commission of 1912. The majority of the royal commission laid down the principle that marriage ought to be dissoluble upon any grounds which frustrated what by universal admission were the fundamental purposes of marriage. I pause to repeat that statement, because it is a rather far-reaching principle.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext: It is the basis of the bill.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext:
It is the fundamental principle of the report of the royal commission, and the basis of the English bill. There are, of course, some who think that marriage can never be dissolved. I am not speaking to that group at the moment. But I am speaking of a situation which exists where divorce is recognized. The idea behind the report of the English commission was that when the very purposes of marriage were frustrated, a divorce was the best possible solution. Let me read that principle again: Marriage ought to be dissoluble upon any grounds which frustrated what by universal admission were

the fundamental purposes of marriage. The preamble to the English act puts its purpose very clearly:
Whereas it is expedient for the* true support of marriage, the protection of children, the removal of hardship, the reduction of illicit unions and unseemly litigation, the relief of conscience among the clergy, and the restoration of due respect for the law, that the acts relating to marriage and divorce be amended.
Then follows the bill. In introducing the measure Colonel Herbert said the bill was to prevent perjury, immorality and collusion, and I am afraid we have had all these evils existing under our mode of procedure here in this parliament. I am not prepared to say to what extent they exist in the courts.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext: And they will continue to exist under this bill.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext:
Well, my hon. friend expresses an opinion, to which of course he is entitled; but that was not the opinion, for instance, of that very representative commission in Great Britain, nor was it the opinion of the majority in the British houses of parliament.
I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that'the constitutionality of the bill was carefuly considered in the senate, whose counsel showed that there was no doubt as to its constitutionality. So I do not think we need pause to-night to discuss that question.
Again let me point out, as is done in the explanatory notes, that the only courts in Canada to which this bill applies are those which now have jurisdiction to decree divorce. We are not setting up any new courts; we are not instituting any new procedure. We are simply dealing with the grounds of divorce in the courts which now have jurisdiction.
The bill deals with divorce, judicial separation, avoidance and alimony, of which, of course, divorce is the most important section. The grounds for divorce are enumerated in section 6:
A petition for divorce may be presented either by the husband or the wife to, and it may be entertained by, the court, on the ground that the respondent:
(a)	has since the celebration of the marriage committed adultery; or
(b)	has deserted the petitioner without cause for a period of at least six years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition; or
(c)	has since the celebration of the marriage treated the petitioner with cruelty; or
(d)	is incurably of unsound mind and has been continuously under care and treatment for a period of at least five years immediately preceding the presentation of the petition.
The first ground, of course, has long been recognized; that is adultery, and I do not

Divorce Causes
intend to enter into a discussion of that ground. The second ground is desertion for six years, which really means seven years before the case can be tried. It has sometimes been charged that the effect of a bill of this kind would be to introduce trial marriage. I do not think anyone can seriously contend that such would be the case. It is only after desertion for seven years that action can be secured. Let me further point out a fact that was new to me. In preparing to present this bill I was reading the Life and Letters of Lord Birkenhead, and I found that since 1573 desertion has been a ground for divorce in Scotland. I do not think anyone can contend that immorality has been more rife in Scotland than elsewhere; that more homes have been broken up in that country, or that there have been any specially injurious results. Yet desertion, a new ground for divorce as far as England was concerned, and as far as this country is concerned, actually has been a ground for divorce in Scotland since 1573.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext: Desertion for what period?

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext: I could not say; I did not look that up.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext: It is very seldom used.

subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR WIDENING OF CAUSES FOR DIVORCE IN CASES BEFORE COURTS
speechtext:
I could not say as to that; but that has been the law, and there is no special reason why it should be used more frequently outside Scotland, except possibly the fact that in this modern day people are travelling about more than they once did.
The third ground is cruelty. Again let me say that some people have become quite frivolous in their explanations as to what constitutes cruelty. I think we need not pay much attention to such objections, because cruelty is defined in the English law in the case of Russell v. Russell,-1897 Appeal Cases, page 395, as follows:
Legal cruelty was conduct of such a character as to cause danger to life and limb or health, bodily or mentally, or such as to give rise to a reasonable apprehension of such danger.
It is only that class of cruelty which can be alleged as a ground for divorce, and that is incorporated in the definitions contained in the bill.
The fourth ground is that a person is of unsound mind. I recognize that possibly there may be some little hesitancy with regard to this, because we all know that some remarkable mental cures are being effected. Yet here it should be noted that it is provided 51952-244
that the patient must have been continuously under care and treatment for a period of at least five years.
I am going to ask the indulgence of the house while I read a paragraph or two from a brilliant speech delivered by Lord Birkenhead on March 24, 1920, during the debate on the matrimonial causes bill. He said:
I, my lords, can only express my amazement that men of saintly lives, men of affairs, men whose opinions and experience we respect, should have concentrated upon adultery as the one circumstance which ought to afford relief from the marriage tie. Adultery is a breach of the carnal obligations of marriage. Insistence upon the duties of continence and chastity is important; it is vital to society. But I have always taken the view that that aspect of marriage was exaggerated and somewhat crudely exaggerated in the marriage service. I am concerned to-day to make this point by which I will stand or fall, that the moral and spiritual sides of marriage are incomparably more important than the physical side. ... If you think of all that marriage means to most of us-the memories of the world's adventure faced together in youth so heedlessly and yet so confidently, the tender comradeship, the sweet association of parenthood, how much more these count than that bond which nature in its ingenious telepathy has contrived to secure and render agreeable, the perpetuation of the species.
And again, in discussing the special case of desertion, particularly as it affects the woman, Lord Birkenhead said:
What is the remedy open to a poor woman who, when she married, gave up the pitiful pursuit by which she made her living until her marriage, and, relying on the marriage, is left penniless, and is left for the whole of her life unable to identify her husband, unable to obtain the slightest relief from the law? She is neither wife nor widow; she has a cold hearthstone; she has fatherless children for the rest of her life. ...	.
In the cases which have come to me within the last fortnight, if I had time to deal with them I could give your Lordships particulars which would bring tears to your eyes. What is a young woman of 22 to do who is, for the rest of her life, with no hope of alleviating the future, with a fugitive husband whom she can never identify, while the law says to her plainly, finally and brutally: "We will do nothing for you." It is said, "You have open to you judicial separation." Choosing my words advisedly and being prepared with chapter and verse of a hundred cases even at a date when the royal commission reported, and in a thousand cases since,. I say that I can prove that this state of judicial separation-admittedly the only alternative-is a hot-bed of vice.
We are told that such a woman as I have described is to remain chaste. I have only to observe that for two thousand years human nature has resisted, in the warmth of youth, these cold admonitions of the cloisters, that I do not believe that the Supreme Being has set a standard which two thousand years of Christian experience has shown that human nature in its exuberant prime cannot support.

Divorce Causes

And one other paragraph also dealing with the question of desertion. This is from Viscount Dawson of Penn:
Passing to clause 2, surely there can be nothing but praise, alike on grounds of logic and humanity, for the granting of divorce for desertion and cruelty. They both frustrate the purposes for which marriage exists. If they exist over years they destroy a marriage and that marriage is not worth preserving. The yielding to a chance physical temptation is as naught compared with the cold calculation of desertion or with a cruelty going on through the years, which can convert a home into a chamber of torments. In my judgment the community has no right to inflict on any human being the continued torture of such a home for any cause whatever.
Since it became known that I had put my name to this bill I have received various letters from people who have told of the desperate straits in which they have been placed, or have urged that some relief be given. I shall quote a sentence or two from the very plain letters of very plain people. Here is a letter from a woman who many years ago had a separation from her husband because of cruelty and non-support. He was a confirmed drunkard. The woman was given custody of the six children, the youngest of whom was only a few months old. All the children are now married. For twenty years the woman has not heard from her husband. She writes:
I am alone now and I have a chance to marry a very good man who would give me a comfortable home, and we would be company for each other in our old age.
I ask the house why she should not be permitted to marry again.
Here is the case of another woman, also elderly, whose husband had given up a position and a salary of So,000 a year. He had allowed all insurance policies to lapse after he had borrowed their full value, and had walked out, leaving his wife and three children penniless. The woman says that she believes she is entitled to a divorce from a man who has treated his wife and children shamefully, and for whom she has neither respect nor liking. She states:
My love died years ago for repeated and various forms of neglect.
Members of the House of Commons, I suggest, ought to try to get away from the involved legal and theological ideas with which we complicate the discussion of this subject. We should come to consider some of the extremely practical cases in actual life which face us at the present time.
Sections 12 and 13 of the bill deal with nullity. I need scarcely direct attention to
fMr, Woodsworth.]
the difference between nullity and divorce. Section 12 specifies these grounds for a decree of nullity:
(a)	that the marriage has not been consummated owing to the wilful refusal of the respondent to consummate it; or
(b)	that either party to the marriage was at the time of the marriage either of unsound mind or a mental defective within the meaning of any statute in force in the province of the court concerned or subject to recurrent fits of insanity or epilepsy; or
(c)	that the respondent was at the time of the marriage suffering from venereal disease of a communicable form; or
(d)	that the respondent was at the' time of the marriage pregnant by some person other than the petitioner.
I need not at the moment go into the other details of the bill which undoubtedly will come to the attention of the house when we reach the committee stage. I think, however, I have presented in as concise form as possible the principles underlying the measure.
I recognize that according to certain theological doctrines marriage is indissoluble. That is a theory which, if consistently held, is worthy of respect, and undoubtedly may retain a very strong hold on people belonging to certain religious faiths. But let me point out that divorce is recognized in this country. Let me point out further that there are divorce courts in nearly every province of the dominion. All this bill attempts to do is to place divorce on a more reasonable basis. My hon. friends who do not agree in principle must remember that in Canada we must work out some sort of modus vivendi.

speechtext:
When this bill last came
up, a point of order was raised by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber), and I now proceed to render my decision upon it.
Bill No. 28, an act to amend the criminal code, was introduced and read the first time on February 24, 1938. It did not then contain explanatory notes as required under the regulations adopted in June, 1923, but the
Criminal Code-Sweepstakes

bill itself was not in imperfect shape. Standing order 70 which prohibits introduction of an imperfect bill was passed on December 20. 1867, long before the adoption of the regulations in respect of explanatory notes on the right hand page. This standing order was probably directed against the introduction of blank bills as often happened in early days. The explanatory notes do not form part of the bill proper and they do not have to be approved by the house. They are only given as reasons for the text and to facilitate discussion.
On May 11 Mr. Bertrand (Laurier), sponsor of this bill, and the only member who had until then spoken to the second reading, asked the law clerks to have it reprinted with explanatory notes in pursuance of my decision on the previous day. He did so under standing order 86, which provides that it shall be the duty of the joint law clerks of the house to assist members of the house in drafting legislation and to revise, print and put notes upon all bills.
The reprint was fully distributed amongst the members of the house on May 13 before debate resumed, so that the regulation of June, 1923, which had been ignored prior to the first reading, was then duly observed. None of the members suffered any prejudice as the bill has been in their hands now for a month and debate has already taken place thereon during four sittings of the house, namely, on May 13, 20 and 31, and June 7.
The practice followed in connection with several government measures and Bill No. 11 which were reprinted with explanatory notes between first and second reading pursuant to my decision of May 10, must also apply in this case. As long as a defect of this nature is corrected before other members than the sponsor have spoken in the debate on the second reading, the rule is sufficiently observed and the bill is in order.
The explanatory notes are of minor importance in this case, but it is necessary to give a decision which will be followed in future.
I therefore rule that the house may proceed with the debate on the second reading of this bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot give a silent vote on this bill, and I propose to give the reasons why I oppose it. I shall endeavour to be brief.
The criminal code of this country, rightly or wrongly, has declared against gambling and lotteries. That represents a crystallized public opinion. That opinion has prevailed

for many years; it is the law of Canada. There are exceptions to that provision. This seeks to extend the exceptions so that lotteries may be held with respect to hospitals and educational institutions. The simple, single question is, is there any warrant for thus interfering with this exception to the generally accepted law of Canada?
Lotteries and gaming are nothing new. They have been before the world for centuries; in fact, games of chance go back to very early days indeed. But the settled experience of mankind has been that they are detrimental alike to the nation and the individual. That is the finding of the world in the light of all these years. Every now and then a nation sets up a commission to investigate, and without exception commissions have found against the continuance of lotteries or gaming. George Washington in one of his letters points out that gaming is framed in avarice, and other great men have pointed out that the effects of it are destructive of the vital character of a people. This is not a question of what my view may be; it is the verdict of the experience of centuries, and that experience is embodied in the criminal code of Canada.
It is suggested that through gambling or lotteries we can make it easy to increase the funds of hospitals. That argument has been adduced in many countries before commissions which have sat upon this question, and for a time, it would seem, the funds have been swollen by the contributions thus received. But in course of time this source of revenue dries up; men and women who were once willing to contribute to charitable objects are no longer inclined to do so; and in the end, it has been found, the state of that community from the standpoint of either hospitals or learning is worse than before it began. Consider the South Sea Bubble, the Great Mississippi question, the Louisiana Lottery; examine these and other similar ventures in the light of what I have said; without a single exception it will be found that they were detrimental to the nation and the individual.
We as legislators are concerned with two things and two only. One has to do with the welfare of the nation, whether or not it is desirable to encourage among the Canadian people the thought that fortunes come by chance, that funds available for learning and for hospitals come by chance, and that because a game of chance will add something to an institution, whether one of learning or a hospital, the individual should take a chance

Supply-Labour-Technical Education
of adding to his personal fortune. Is this the time to encourage that attitude of mind? I think not.
I could elaborate by extensive quotations and by what I conceive to be fairly logical arguments why, from the standpoint of the nation, this proposal should not be adopted. But, sir, the case as it affects the individual is yet stronger. What habit does it encourage in the individual? It conduces to unemployment, because men are ever seeking to get money to buy a sweepstake ticket. I am not unmindful of the tremendous pressure brought to bear upon many of us to support this sort of thing. Other men may have convictions quite as strong as mine, and I give the same measure of respect to their convictions as I hope they do to mine. But when I say to an individual, "Yes, we are going to encourage sweepstakes in Canada so that you may be able to beg, and sometimes"-as commissions have made clear- ''you may go so far as to steal to buy tickets on those sweepstakes," I am encourage-ing him to risk all upon a hope which is but a vain delusion; for it has been established beyond all question that never was there a vainer delusion than the belief that in the end you can get rich by chance.	,

Over the week-end of May 21-24 there met in Toronto the Third Canadian Youth Congress. During the course of their deliberations they prepared various resolutions, among them one on vocational guidance, which I should like to read:
The present trend for more technical training in our schools increases the need for trained vocational counsellors. These counsellors can assist students in choosing an occupation to which they will be suited and from which they will be able to derive an adequate livelihood. Statistics regarding trends in employment, opportunities in industry, as gathered by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, should be placed at the disposal of vocational counsellors. The employment of such counsellors in our schools should be encouraged.
In view of the costly labour turn-over and unfitness due to the lack of direction, trained vocational counsellors should be included on the staffs of government employment bureaus, in order that the percentage of permanent placements may be increased.
I think one may recognize the sincerity of that resolution and also the fact that it makes a suggestion which is most worthy. One of the reasons why I was asking the minister the questions I did a few moments ago, under

Supply-Labour-Technical Education
this item dealing with technical education, was that I was wondering whether it would not be possible to find funds for the purpose suggested by the resolution. Those of us who have had dealings with the younger generation realize how often they are ill advised in regard to the courses they should follow. Our technical schools are doing a magnificent job. There are enrolled in these schools some 125,000 or 130,000 young people, many of whom are not altogether sure as to what courses they should follow. Accordingly there is placed upon the principals and teachers a rather difficult problem, in view of the numbers with which they have to deal. They do not know the personnel of their student body as fully as they might. I was going to say as fully as they should, but that is hardly fair, because they do the best they can, and they do it well; but they do not know the individual students as fully as others might if they were rendering assistance directly in connection with this work, such as the assistance that might be rendered by a counsellor. I wondered if the minister had given any thought to the idea that perhaps it would be desirable to make contact, perhaps through the youth committee, with the various technical schools across the dominion, with the view of placing counsellors here and there in some of the larger centres.

I find no fault whatever
with the terms of the resolution to which my hon. friend has referred. He would be the first to agree, I think, that the resolution should be addressed to the provinces as well as to the dominion.
Quite.

Indeed, under the easting organization of the employment service I should say the responsibility of appointing additional vocational officers would rest rather upon the provinces than upon the dominion. As I mentioned this afternoon, it is the intention of the government in connection with the training projects for unemployed young people to appoint special placement officers in the various provinces, who will be in close touch with the facilities for technical education and also with the offices of the Employment Service of Canada. I feel that probably this would meet the immediate situation.

I thought perhaps the advisers or counsellors would deal more with those seeking employment than with^ those seeking some course of education; but if it is the plan that they will work in close contact with the technical schools, of course that answers my question.

When I say they will
work in close contact with the schools, that is in the sense that technical schools would be used and have been used to some extent in connection with the training plans for unemployed young people.

I do not know whether I have missed the discussion I wish to raise or whether it has been raised already, but several times I have heard men say that there is a demand in Canada for skilled workmen, for which there is not a sufficient supply.
I have heard this on fairly good authority.
I am wondering whether the minister has any means of determining just what may be the nature of that demand. For example, is there any means whereby anyone in a school in Manitoba could find out just in what kind of skilled labour there is a deficiency in the dominion? I had the matter brought to my attention several times while the highly commendable work of the minister in giving special training to young people was in progress, that probably the young people did not know what to prepare for, and had no idea whether or not there would be a demand for them when they were trained. I was just wondering if the minister had adopted some definite plan in this regard and, if he had, what means he had adopted for advertising the fact so that those in need of the information might readily acquire it.

In each province the
employment office would have a record of applications by employers for additional help, and we have also a record of those who had registered in these various trades, so a study of those two records would enable the employment service in a province to determine whether there was a special demand for a certain type of mechanical training. I remember some years ago hearing, in connection with technical education, of one province -at the moment I have forgotten which- that felt there was a demand for telegraph operators, and they turned out a very large number of telegraph operators, far more than could possibly be absorbed. Obviously that was a mistake. In connection with our training projects for unemployed young people we are trying to avoid that by applying training only in those fields where there is either an immediate or a prospective demand for employment.

To give a specific case, it was brought to my attention the other day by a statement from a young man who not long ago had come from .Germany, that there was a distinct dearth in Canada of skilled toolmakers, and that anyone who was really

Supply-Labour-Technical Education
proficient in that kind of work could readily find employment in Canada at good remuneration. I thought that was most remarkable. Here we have thousands of boys eager to get some sort of work that can be depended upon, and here we have a demand that is not being supplied. I wonder what provision we have for stopping up that gap.
There is another matter to which I should like to refer. I may say that I am very much interested in this question, having been a school principal for a good many years. I am sincerely and sympathetically interested in the minister's work, and I am well pleased with the efforts he has made. It is not well known how long it takes to train for some of these occupations, and there are vocations which require something in the nature of apprenticeship. It would greatly assist many of our boys if they knew what firms were prepared to take apprentices, what the conditions would be and how long it would take them to qualify.
There is another matter which, I think, must be cleared up very soon. I have mentioned it several times, and I mean to speak sympathetically, though I intend to be emphatic. It is this. There is altogether too widespread a belief, loosely entertained, that in this country there is work which can be obtained. I find that belief on every hand among the more prosperous, well-equipped, well-to-do people, who are not really in contact with realities. In order to get an accurate knowledge of just to what extent there are or can be jobs, this sort of service is particularly valuable. I hope I make my meaning clear to the minister; I should like to hear him speak in this regard.

As to the first question,
I believe it to be true that there is a dearth of toolmakers in Canada. I cannot speak positively on that point, but I have understood that in connection with the aeronautical industry, for instance, it has been found that there is an insufficient supply of well-trained machinists. A number of these industries that are now going into aeroplane production are themselves arranging for apprenticeships. I think it must be recognized that this field is not one which belongs exclusively to governments. In Great Britain, as the hon. member is no doubt aware, an apprenticeship system has been established over a long period of time. That is carried out jointly by the industries and the trade unions. In this country there has not been as much interest in apprenticeship as one might have wished. I believe I am correct in saying that at the 
present time only three provinces have apprenticeship legislation. I may point out that other provinces are expressing an interest in the apprenticeship system, and we hope that similar legislation may be passed in those provinces in the very near future.
As to the second question, I believe there can be no doubt at all that the man who trains himself for a particular job, provided there is a reasonable expectation of a demand for such a job, is in an infinitely better position during a period of unemployment than is one who has no special training. That is one reason, among others, why in the training projects for unemployed young people we are doing whatever can be done within the limits of the appropriation voted by parliament to provide occupational training in the various cities. I shall not say that up to the present time we have done more than make a modest contribution to the problem; but I think what has been done is an indication of the wisdom of pursuing the policy, and I hope it may be extended as time goes on.

I am more interested in the means by which one may get information. Supposing I am the principal of a school-as I was, before I was elected-and I wish to know just where a particularly bright boy might be taken on as an apprentice, or what kind of technical training he might get in Calgary or some other centre, in order to qualify for admission to apprenticeship; where and by what means at the present time can I get information so as to guide that boy?

I would say the first
application should be made to the provincial employment office. That would be done to determine where there would be a greater likelihood of a boy trained in a certain mechanical trade being absorbed. An application could be also made directly to the larger industries in the province. The truth of the matter is that our industries are under no compulsion to register with the employment service. Registration is a purely voluntary arrangement, so that it might very well be that the information which would come from the employment service would not be conclusive.

If a boy in northern British Columbia wishes to qualify as a toolmaker, for instance, and if he applied to an employment bureau in that province, is there a strong likelihood that they would know of the needs in Ottawa, or in any of the

Supply-Labour-Technical Education
industrial centres of Ontario or eastern Canada? Is the need registered in Ontario and transmitted to British Columbia, so that the officials in the latter province may know? I believe one of the reasons we are not as effective in the matter of apprenticeship is that distances are so tremendously great, as compared with those in Great Britain. Therefore we need to be particularly careful in getting details.

I believe that is undoubtedly true. The difficulties of carrying out apprenticeship here are greater because of the distances involved. Each provincial employment office may secure information with respect to employment opportunities in other provinces. That is one of the purposes carried out by the dominion coordination branch of the Employment Service of Canada. Therefore there would be no reason why an employment office in British Columbia could not or would not be advised of possible employment opportunities in a particular trade in Ontario or Quebec.
Would it be advised through the minister's department?
It would be advised through the clearing-house here.

Is it not a fact that in Ontario information is readily obtainable through a system of inspectorships which have been established by the government of Ontario with respect not only to apprenticeships but to leamerships as well?
I believe that is correct.

I think the minister will admit that there have been very few apprenticeships through employment bureaux. A very small percentage of employers make application to employment bureaux for employees. In support of my colleague I should like to repeat a conversation I had a year ago with one of the chief engineers of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He told me that when they were building stream-lined trains in Canada they could not obtain tradesmen or mechanics qualified to carry out the work, and I understand they had to import them from the United States. Of course, that is a terrible state of affairs.
During the period of depression in Great Britain they had a system of youth training, and I say that system is long overdue in Canada. If in the last seven years we had developed the natural ability of people between the ages of eighteen and twenty-five,
we would have built up a great national asset for the future. I do not think it is too late to begin.
There are in Canada trade schools qualified to teach various trades. Unfortunately, however, it has been learned that the activities of some of them have been more or less fraudulent, and some have acted under false pretences. That is by no means true of all of them. Unfortunately, provincial legislatures have passed legislation making it impossible in some instances for these schools to operate. I wonder if the minister would not give consideration to the establishment across Canada of a system of youth training so that the youth of the country may have an opportunity. Certainly they have not in the last six or seven years had an opportunity to learn a trade. When they are trained to a point where they are useful to industry they will be ready to slip into available positions. I say it is a scathing indictment against us to find that we had to import mechanics at a time when there were thousands of unemployed in Canada. Some appropriation should be made to see that these trades are kept right up to date, and that the men have an opportunity to learn mechanical engineering, and other types of work.

Is the hon. member aware that last year parliament appropriated a million dollars for the precise purpose he has in mind? That amount was not entirely expended, but the amount that was expended -and we shall be dealing with it later-was duplicated by the provinces. In the hon. member's native province of Alberta, for instance, an excellent work was done under the superintendence of Doctor McNally of the board of education. Certainly we propose to extend the work during the present year.
What trades were covered?
I have not that information before me, but I would suggest that this discussion might proceed more properly under an item in the supplementary estimates, and we can deal with it there.
Is the amount authorized by statute a balance that remains over from a sum that was voted some years ago, and allotted to each province? Which provinces have used up their amounts?

Probably the hon. member was not in the house when I gave that information. All the provinces except Manitoba have used their amounts, and this amount is available for that province.

At page 12 of the interim report of the national employment commission I find this:
The commission recommended the following as a basis upon which such plans should be framed:
Training projects of an occupational nature;
Short-term learnership courses not exceeding one year in duration, devised to provide theoretical training concurrent with specific employment;
Work projects incorporating re-conditioning, training, and conservation features, for the purposes of restoring morale and of conserving natural resources.
Then on page 39 of the main report appear these words:
An adequate supply of skilled or semi-skilled labour is an essential at all times_ for the efficient carrying on of commercial, industrial and agricultural or other primary activities. The number of unskilled workers that can be placed in employment depends, to a considerable extent, upon the adequacy with which this requirement for the more skilled worker can be met.
There are two main phases to the work of training which fall within the commission's purview:
1.	Rehabilitation work arising out of the necessities of intermittent period of economic stress;
2.	Pei'manent training measures, e.g., apprenticeship and learnership, applicable at all times.
In both cases it would seem proper that the main responsibility (other than that which falls on industry itself) for providing adequate measures suitable to the varying conditions in the different provinces should lie with the province in question. It is not suggested by the commission that jurisdiction in these matters should be assumed either in whole or in part by the dominion, except that, when special need exists as at present, or as it may in similar future periods of economic stress, the dominion might contribute towards the cost of particular rehabilitation or training projects.
That is all I can find in either the interim or the final report dealing with vocational training as carried out in technical schools. I wonder if any other reports have been made by the national employment commission and particularly by the youth training committee of that commission dealing with this particular phase of the matter? The Technical Education Act was very successful in establishing technical education in the provinces. This act was so acceptable to the provinces that perhaps we are missing an opportunity here to carry forward a work which has been in progress now for a matter of nineteen years and which has given such extraordinarily satisfactory results. I was wondering why the national employment commission omitted that phase of the work from their report.

My hon. friend will recall that it was as a result of the recommendation of the national employment commission, following the report of the youth employment committee to the commission, that the special item of $1,000,000 was placed in the estimates last year for training projects for unemployed young people. The report of the youth employment committee was not made to the minister or the government; it was a report of a general nature made to the commission. Many such reports of a special nature were made to the commission. The commission went over this material and derived from it the recommendations which appeared in the interim and subsequently in the final report.

In a debate some weeks ago I referred to this particular item which used to appear in much larger figures in the annual estimates. I deplored the fact that the amount granted was not as large as previously. I recognize the fact that education comes primarily within the jurisdiction of the provinces, but this is one instance where the federal government has been able to assist materially in a work under provincial control. It has been my observation that those small cities having technical schools suffered less during the depression.
I am thinking particularly of Shawinigan Falls in Quebec where a technical school was started many years ago by the Shawinigan Water and Power Company. Later on the school received assistance from the Quebec government and the city of Shawinigan Falls. This school also received a tremendous impetus from the grant given by the federal government under this legislation which is about to pass out of existence. This technical school in Shawinigan Falls offers an outstanding example, not only to the province of Quebec but to Canada as a whole. French and English boys are able to receive a technical education after having obtained a primary education in their own schools or classical colleges. The result is that the labour market in and around Shawinigan Falls is well supplied with trained labour. These boys attend technical school for a certain number of years and then are absorbed into the various industries in Shawinigan Falls, Grand-Mere, Three Rivers and other places. The school is operated also in the evenings, and many of the boys continue their education at those classes. Many of these boys, by reason of the technical education they have received, have risen in the community to high positions which they otherwise would not have been able to attain.

I know it is difficult to find money, but I believe curtailment could be made in other directions and the necessary money found to apply to this particular field. As an educationalist I recognize the value of this type of education. In this country we have overemphasized classical and academic training, and in certain provinces we have no provision for the vocational and technical training of young boys and girls. I think this is an opportunity for the federal government to supplement any local efforts which are being made.

I know the conditions which prevailed in that part of the country during the depression, and if the hon. member who represents that district is in the chamber, I know he will bear out what I say. They did not feel the full effect of the depression because most of the boys had received technical training after their regular education. Many of them continued attending evening classes until they found work in some of the industries. The result was that these boys were not roaming around the country in an effort to find work. They were
improving themselves and getting ready for something better in the future. You may say they could have done that equally well in a classical college or academic institution, but that is not so. I would urge upon the minister, first, that the withdrawal of this grant has placed an additional burden of taxation on localities or on provinces to maintain what was started or, at all events, received an impetus as a result of the previous grant, and, second, I would stress the good work that could be done if this grant were continued, in view of the developments which are taking place in certain of our industrial centres. New industrial centres are springing up here and there throughout the country. I have in mind one, a tremendous development, which opened only last week in the province of Quebec, and within a short time it will no doubt receive the benefit of provincial assistance in erecting a technical school. I was glad when I heard the minister deal with that phase and suggest that the person trained for a job has less difficulty in finding work than one who has received just a general training without any particular line of work in view, and I feel that the only way in which we can give that definite training is by the establishment of technical or vocational schools. Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to make a speech nor am I going to, neither do I wish to hold up these estimates. The hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) has just made many remarks that I was going to make on this item.
I think all of us who have had to do with Young Canada, particularly in the last few years, realize without any question whatsoever in our minds that the most practical contribution which can be made to the development of the young man or young woman who has some idea of gaining the most useful information possible in the way of development, and so forth, can be given by our technical schools, and therefore I think it is very unfortunate, after all the provinces, I believe, until 1929 were still participating in this plan in view of the fact that the Technical Education Act was extended for a further five years, that this work contributed to by the dominion government should be handicapped by the fact that its contribution is no longer forthcoming.
The hon. member for Mount Royal states that the municipalities have been forced to extend taxation in order to carry on this work and to take up the slack occasioned by the fact that this grant was not forthcoming from the federal government. If he will permit me to differ, I think he will find that instead of further municipal taxes being collected for this purpose the work was simply not carried on to the same degree as it had been in the past with the assistance of the dominion government's contribution, and when that grant was no longer received the work more or less ceased at that point.
The records will show, as the minister well knows, that technical education has been taken advantage of by increasing numbers of our young people throughout the years, and particularly from 1919 on. Apprenticeships, no matter how well organized they may be, can never fully take the place of technical education or education in the technical schools. After all, the boy who goes to work in a shop, even with the best available instruction, is deprived of the theory which is back of the practice in which he is engaged. In the shop he is taught practice rather than theory, whereas in the technical school he has theory and practice together; then later when he gets himself a job, wherever it may be, he starts with a definite amount of theory and a certain amount of practice, and then added to that theory and practice comes 
the experience within the shop itself. Therefore the apprenticeship courses which in great part no longer exist, and which have recently been revised as a result of the activities of the past year, never will, no matter how well organized they may be, take the place of the technical education which the lad or young girl gets in a technical school.
I therefore earnestly urge on the minister that he again give consideration to introducing a technical education act to function as the past act did. Here we find ourselves facing a " sure thing," if I may use the phrase; for we realize, as a result of experience over a matter now of some nineteen years, that the purpose to which these funds are devoted is a worthy and worth while purpose and has accomplished a definite job of work which has been most beneficial not only to the individual but to the community in which he lives.
The projects which have been launched under the youth training plan, which we shall come to shortly in the supplementary estimates, are in a very great degree experimental, and the minister will admit that some have proven to be better than others. On the other hand, here we are dealing with a project that is no longer speculative but has proven to be of value. The provinces have been accustomed to accepting this grant, to accepting it gratefully, and to bear their own share, and therefore there is no difficulty whatsoever about cooperation with the provinces in regard to this matter. There was no pious hope that this or that province would accept the grant even though it had at first refused it, or whatever the case may have been. Accordingly, Mr. Chairman, in view of our experience under the act and the results that were obtained, I urge upon the minister with all the earnestness of which I am capable that he give consideration to bringing down next session a new technical education act, to function as the old.

May I add a brief word on one particular phase which probably has not been referred to in the discussion so far. Under the Technical Education Act technical schools have been started and maintained over a period of years in some of the larger urban centres, assisted by the provinces to a very great extent at the beginning, to the extent probably of fifty per cent for equipment, and with large grants for teachers' salaries, but as the years went on these grants have gradually been cut off. Technical education has been established as a necessary form of education. I think everyone who has experience will admit that. Now, as the years roll by, the grants from the provinces have

The minister spoke on the question of the increased rates. There has been some controversy, as the minister knows, with respect to that matter. On what principle are the rates increased? That was the special work undertaken by Professor Mackenzie of the university of Toronto, a very well known actuary, who I believe had served as special actuary of one of the Carnegie foundations. Upon his advice we made an interim increase in* the rates amounting to fifteen per cent. That was put into effect

This matter raises the

As I understand Professor Mackenzie's work, he took the last British tables, but he did not apply them in terms of premiums but, because of our experience, made a lesser premium than they would call for. He did not, however, purport to do it in a completely scientific manner. I read a criticism of it on that basis. I think what he did was a perfectly sound thing; he gave us the benefit of an arbitrary basis because of our decreased mortality or increased length of life as compared with the British table. The result is that to-day our rates are still somewhat lower than rates based upon the purely British actuarial basis or the United States expectation of life, either one; quite substantially lower in some instances.
The point which I think does arise is the question of the interest rate. We predicate the rate upon the fact that the entire fund is in the consolidated revenue fund, and that the nation itself will pay interest on that money; the interest used* to be at the rate of four per cent.

We tested the fitness of several tables and found that the mortality rates of the new British offices tables, known as the a(m) and a (f) tables were, when taken at ages one year younger than the actual ages for each sex, more nearly in safe agreement with the experience under investigation than any other standard rates. The number of deaths among male lives over age fifty-five which actually occurred is five per cent less than the number "expected" by the a(m) table at tabular ages, but three per cent greater than the number expected when ages are rated down one year. The number of deaths among female lives over age fifty-five which actually occurred is four per cent less than the number expected by the a(f) table at tabular ages, but five and a half per cent greater than the number expected when ages are rated down one year. We have therefore decided to recommend the adoption of the a(m) and a(f) tables with a reduction of one year in age, which means that calculations on a life aged sixty-five for example will be made as if the life were aged sixty-four.

Special-To provide for commitments under relief settlement agreements with provincial governments, $200,000.

Would the minister
kindly explain this item?
51952-245i

This amount of $200,000 is needed to provide for commitments under relief settlement agreements with the provincial governments. It will be remembered that these relief settlement agreements were entered into with a number of the provinces by the previous administration. The purpose of the agreement was to take families who were on relief and place them on selected farms. This was a tripartite arrangement under which contributions were made by the dominion, the province and the municipality concerned. At first these agreements were entered into with most of the provinces, but at the present time the only provinces to which we are contributing are Quebec, Manitoba and Alberta. The total of $200,000 now asked for is accounted for by the following requirements:
Quebec	$100,000
Manitoba	 80,000
Alberta	  20,000
Contributions are made by the municipality concerned, the province and the dominion?
Yes. The intention is to take families on relief, place them on farm land and provide assistance for a period of four years in order that the family may be able to establish itself.

What progress has been
made in this regard in British Columbia?

Very few have actually
been placed in British Columbia. The total number covered by agreements in British Columbia is 285, made up of fifty-two families and 233 dependents.
I notice this is a revote; was it unexpended last year?
The agreements were entered into in 1936. They are four-year agreements, and our commitments are determined upon the number of families actually placed.
What is the situation with respect to Ontario?
The agreement with Ontario has expired, but the numbers placed under previous agreements were 606 families with 2,384 dependents, making a total of 2,990 persons. They were placed from 1932 to 1934.

There has been no
continuation of that agreement?

No. That plan has not
been continued in Ontario.
The provincial government does not want to negotiate, is that it?

They have not expressed a desire to revive the agreement for this purpose.

I notice the item under consideration is a revote. What was the amount voted last year, of which the revote now is $200,000? I assume the minister will be able to tell how much was expended out of last year's vote.
The amount voted for this purpose last year was $400,000.

How much of that was spent? Was it $200,000? Possibly I could make the point on which I am seeking information a little clearer to the minister. Take another department, the Department of Public Works, for instance. We vote, we will say, $100,000 for a building this year. When you come to the end of the year you have spent only, say, $50,000, and you wish to complete the building. Then you have by way of revote the balance of the original $100,000, which would be $50,000 to revote. Does the minister mean by a revote here a reappropriation of part of a vote of last year? Is this a new vote or a voting again of something that has already been voted?
The amount voted last year was $400,000.
If we are revoting $200,000 this year, then approximately $200,000 was spent last year.

I am just trying to get the information. The actual expenditures are made under the terms of agreements. The agreements are not limited to a specific number of families, except as to a maximum, so it is not always possible to tell in advance how much will be expended. Perhaps we might let the item stand, and I shall see that the information is brought down.
Will the minister also be good enough to tell the committee how much was spent on each family? Does it depend on the farm to which they are going?

The dominion pays one-third of an amount not in excess of $1,000

with respect to the settlement of families on land from organized municipalities who would otherwise be in receipt of direct relief. The agreement also provides for a fifty per cent contribution by the dominion not in excess of S300 per family taken from an unorganized district. That is extended for a period of four years. Under what item may we discuss contributions to the provinces in aid of public works?
I think the appropriate item will be the next one, No. 517.

My reason for seeking information was that the same question arises under three votes, Nos. 516, 517 and 518, and what I am anxious to ascertain is just what " revote " means. Is it a revote of the amount that was originally appropriated and that has not been exhausted, or is it a new vote altogether?

It is really a revote of the amount to which we were committed under the agreement made subject to the legislation of last, year, and which we were not called upon to pay. I am not sure that a revote in that sense is a revote in the sense in which it is generally understood and applied in the Department of Public Works.

That is exactly what I was trying to make clear to the committee. These items are not revotes in the ordinary sense of the word to which we have been accustomed in connection with public works estimates. It seems to be the voting of a similar item to last year, but unless it is part of an appropriation of last year I believe it is not really a revote at all, but a new vote.
I think it would be fair to say that certainly the first and the second and the third are votes to provide payment for commitments made last year.

That is what I thought; but unless, as I say, it is part of the same item that was voted last year, it is not strictly correct to call it a revote. It is a vote to meet obligations that will mature during this year under agreements that were made last year, or possibly prior to that.
Item stands.
To provide for commitments and completion of works in connection with federal contributions to provincial and municipal relief projects, $1,075,000.

How much by way of contributions to British Columbia has been
voted by this government, we will say in the last five years?
I shall be glad to take note of that question. I am quite sure that this item will not pass to-night because there will be some further discussion on it.

While the minister is looking that up, will he also look up whether the government is going to give that money-
I know it is $33,000,000-to the province, or will it expect the province to repay it?
Is my hon. friend now referring to loans or to actual contributions made by the dominion government to British Columbia for joint works over a period of five years?

Well, I am referring to the matter of $33,000,000, of which about $3,000,000 has been repaid in some way, I do not know how. I am asking the question particularly for the reason that for almost everything which is lacking funds for the purpose of completion the federal government is blamed if it does not come through with the money. But I have before me a press dispatch in which the finance minister at Victoria makes the statement that he does not expect the federal government to demand repayment of this money, or to collect this money.
I shall be glad to secure that information for my hon. friend and to make it available when we are in committee again on this item.

What public works are being undertaken in British Columbia, either by the dominion government, or by this government in conjunction with the provincial government, on which the unemployed men who are in the Vancouver post office and in the art gallery can be placed?

Well, there are no joint works to which the dominion government is now contributing through the Department of Labour. There are two stretches of highway, the Big Bend highway and the new highway from the international border to New Westminster, either to which the dominion government is contributing or for which there has been an undertaking that the dominion government will contribute.
Is that under this vote? Mr. ROGERS: It is not under this vote at all, no.

Those are the only two projects on which these unemployed men could be placed at work?

Supply-Labour-Reliej Projects

Oh, no, I would not say that, because a number of other public works projects of the various departments-the Department of Transport, for instance, and the Department of (Public Works-are being carried out in various parts of the province. My hon. friend has raised his question rather under the Department of Labour votes, and I am able to tell him only with regard to the votes that are given here. As a matter of fact, although last year our contributions to highways were under the Department of Labour, this year they are rather under the Department of Mines and Resources, and to some extent under the Department of Transport in so far as our contributions pertain to the abolition of level crossings.

I take it that the minister is very much concerned to have these men working, or at least to offer them work. Can they be placed on the work on the Big Bend highway and on the road from the boundary to New Westminster? If so, I suggest that this information be conveyed to them at once. If that were done, we might get quite a number of them out of the post office and the art gallery, and public support would be swung behind the government instead of, as I think it is to-day, being largely behind the men because it is felt that nothing is being done. The tragedy is that no move whatever is being made by this government. At least that is the feeling in Vancouver. Cannot the minister take some step to offer these men work right away on these two highways?

The work on the Big Bend highway has been continued over a period of years under agreement with British Columbia. The work on the highway from the international boundary to New Westminster has not yet been started. In all probability it will be done as a joint project with British Columbia. I believe an announcement has already been made with regard to that work, and it has been stated that those who are single and unemployed and residents in British Columbia will be upon the same footing as others as to eligibility for this work, but I am not saying and could not say that there would be an opportunity on this work for all those who are at present unemployed in the city of Vancouver.

Could the minister
give us in regard to Alberta similar information to what he has just given with respect to British Columbia?

There is nothing in these votes, at least in the particular vote that is before us, for Alberta. My hon. friend is really now asking me to speak from memory fMr. Green.]
of votes in other departments. I happened to recall the vote for the Big Bend highway in British Columbia and the highway from the international boundary.
Can he tell us under which item we can discuss this?
The matter can be discussed under Ne 517, the item now before the committee.
How much of this amount of $1,075,000 is allocated to British Columbia and what projects will be carried out under the vote?
